title: Building a Better Bar: The Twelve Building Blocks of Minimum Competence
pub: IAALS, the Institute for the Advancement of the American Legal System (University of Denver)
author: Deborah Jones Merritt · Logan Cornett

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal careers: Mobility coexists with sector barriers
st.an: The source does not assess whether mobility coexists with durable sector barriers or whether credentials and social background shape career allocation and rewards. It only supplies methodological context about counting employment settings and matching an external comparison group, which is relevant to the cluster’s measurement caveats but insufficient to establish a position on its principal proposition.
qs: Sixteen of the junior lawyers in our study worked in two different settings during their first year of practice, so the total number of employment settings is 217 rather than 201.

Columns four and five contrast those numbers with data reported by the National Association for Law Placement (NALP) for the class of 2017, the modal year in which our junior lawyers earned their law degrees.76 We filtered the NALP data to include only jobs that required bar admission, because our study included only lawyers with jobs that required a license.77

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI directly, but materially strengthens the cluster’s distinction between bounded task performance and general legal competence. Its empirical account shows that competent practice integrates contextual issue identification, client interaction, judgment, strategy, communication and workload management—capabilities that support selective, human-led deployment and cannot be inferred from isolated task gains.
qs: More than five dozen distinct competencies, in fact, outranked knowledge of doctrinal law as necessary in the short term.

Issue identification in practice requires critical thinking skills, an understanding of threshold concepts in many practice areas, and the ability to interact with a client or supervisor in a way that brings hidden issues to light.

st.t: Effective help: Justice outcomes outrank lawyer supply
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s evidence-based orientation by identifying the lack of systematic research on minimum lawyer competence and advocating evidence-based licensing assessment. Its contribution is narrower than the cluster’s user-outcome framework and does not compare lawyers with lay assistance, procedural reform or technology, nor demonstrate justice outcomes.
qs: Background                                         Prior Research Surprisingly few studies have probed the knowledge and skills that new lawyers need to represent clients competently.
8 ^Lan evidence-based licensing system, together with three examples of systems that could effectively assess the building blocks of minimum competence.

st.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s methodological qualification that employment comparisons depend on consistent definitions and representative samples. Its exclusion of clerkships, deliberate oversampling of solo practitioners, and acknowledged underrepresentation of the largest firms constrain generalisation, though it does not independently address the claimed entry-level contraction or its causes.
qs: We excluded judicial clerkships from counts of new-lawyer jobs in this table and elsewhere.
Second, that focus (combined with some self-selection) led to underrepresentation of lawyers working at the largest law firms.

st.t: Research representation: Purposeful samples limit wider claims
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: it treats participant diversity as valuable for qualitative inquiry while documenting purposeful sampling, demographic and employment-setting imbalances, missing perspectives, and unavailable national comparators that limit broader generalisation.
qs: The study was not designed to detect any differences in participant perspectives based on age, gender, race/ethnicity, or first- generation status; for our purposes, it was important only to include diverse voices from these categories.

About an eighth specified regulatory work and 3.0% indicated that at least some of their practice fell in the “other” category.78 We could not find comparable data for lawyers nationally, so we cannot compare our participants to the broader population.

kp.k: Licensing needs an evidence-based definition of minimum competence
kp.d: The authors argue that bar examinations cannot credibly protect the public without an empirically grounded definition of entry-level competence. Correlations with law school grades and LSAT scores do not establish competence for practice. They frame licensing as a balance between screening out incompetent representation and avoiding protectionist or discriminatory barriers.
qs: The unfortunate reality is that, although the bar exam has existed for more than a century, there has never been an agreed-upon, evidence-based definition of minimum competence.
Professional licensing systems attempt to shield the public from incompetent practitioners, but they can also harm consumers by insulating professions from unwanted competition.

kp.k: National qualitative research examines first-year practice
kp.d: The study conducted 50 focus groups between August 12, 2019, and May 27, 2020, across 18 locations in 12 states: 41 groups of junior lawyers and nine of supervisors. Including one individual interview, the dataset comprised 201 participants—159 junior lawyers and 42 supervisors—and more than 75 hours of transcribed discussions. Analysis used grounded theory, iterative coding, and checks for conflicting viewpoints. The sample deliberately emphasized some underrepresented perspectives and solo practice; it was not designed to estimate national prevalence or demographic differences, and disability, religion, and sexual orientation were not collected.
qs: After adding that interview to the database, we had a total of 201 participants: 159 junior lawyers and 42 supervisors.
Forty of the groups met in person, while ten convened virtually after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
At the same time, we searched for conflicting viewpoints and noted them where applicable.

kp.k: Competence comprises twelve interdependent capabilities
kp.d: The authors propose twelve building blocks: professional conduct; understanding legal processes and sources; threshold concepts; interpreting legal materials; client interaction; issue identification; research; lawyerly communication; understanding the big picture; workload management; coping with stress; and self-directed learning. They argue that all are necessary before licensing and that together they support practice with little supervision and continuing development. This is a proposed competence framework grounded in participants’ accounts, rather than a validated predictive assessment.
qs: By analyzing the insights of our focus group members, we identified 12 interconnected competencies—which we term “building blocks”—that allowed them to practice effectively.
We propose that possession of these building blocks constitutes minimum competence: new lawyers who possess these building blocks are able to represent clients with little or no supervision.
A serious licensing system, one focused on protecting the public, cannot omit essential competencies simply because they are difficult to test.

kp.k: Practice demands adaptability rather than memorized rules
kp.d: Participants and supervisors emphasized foundational understanding, source checking, and learning rather than reliance on rules memorized for examinations. The authors distinguish threshold concepts—transformative understanding of a field’s principles and policies—from detailed jurisdiction-specific rules. They also distinguish memory acquired through repeated practice, which may improve efficiency, from short-term examination memorization. Their review of earlier studies similarly finds cognitive skills more central than recall.
qs: Our research suggests that new lawyers do not rely upon a static set of legal rules and skills carried into the workplace.
This building block focuses on understanding principles and policies that govern the law, rather than memorizing specific black-letter rules.
Deep familiarity with legal principles gained through hands-on practice helped lawyers become more efficient.

kp.k: Federal-focused preparation mismatches varied state and local practice
kp.d: Almost half of participants worked exclusively or primarily with state and local law, and a similar proportion used a mixture of state, local, and federal law. Participants described more than 50 practice fields; 41.5% of junior lawyers changed jobs, while pro bono work and varied assignments also broadened practice. The authors associate federal-centered preparation with reported errors involving state rules and authority. They support portability through uniform examinations but argue that assessment must reflect state and local law, administrative agencies, legislation, and alternative dispute resolution.
qs: Almost half of participants indicated that they worked exclusively or primarily with state and local law.
A similar proportion worked with a mixture of state, local, and federal law.

New lawyers, they suggested, hold a warped view of the legal system in which federal law dwarfs state and local law, while courts overshadow legislatures, agencies, and alternative dispute resolution processes.

kp.k: Limited supervision exposes clients to junior lawyers’ gaps
kp.d: Although some participants reported supportive training, a majority described substantial responsibility with little or no supervision, especially in smaller firms, government, and nonprofits; some large-firm lawyers reported similar experiences. Supervisors acknowledged time constraints and deficiencies in feedback skills. Reported errors included an unreviewed damages calculation that reduced an arbitration award. The authors conclude that licensing should reflect actual limited supervision rather than assume employers will supply missing competence.
qs: A majority of new lawyers, however, described workplaces where they assumed substantial responsibility for client matters with little or no supervision.
Supervisors also recognized that many of them lacked effective feedback skills.
the licensing system should assume lack of supervision: that is the reality in the workplace.

kp.k: Solo practice does not necessarily mean unsupported practice
kp.d: The study deliberately oversampled solos: 10.4% of participants started solo practice during their first year, versus 1.9% of 2017 graduates in the report’s comparison of jobs requiring bar admission. Several used incubators, shared offices, or mentoring networks; more than half concentrated on a single field. The authors caution against assuming that all new solos are isolated generalists, while noting their need for business preparation.
qs: Several of the solo practitioners in our study began their work within incubators.
That setting gave them ongoing access to mentors, specialized instruction, and practitioner networks.
More than half focused their services on a single area, such as immigration, family law, estate planning, or criminal defense.

kp.k: Client interaction is an entry-level professional capability
kp.d: Substantial client contact was common among participants, including in some large firms, and supervisors wanted client-centered thinking even where direct contact was limited. New lawyers reported inadequate preparation for building trust, gathering facts, identifying goals, counseling, managing expectations, delivering bad news, and working across differences in background or disability. Reported mistakes illustrate that these are legally consequential abilities rather than generic interpersonal skills.
qs: Client contact, in sum, is commonplace for new lawyers.
New lawyers need more than simple “people skills”; they need the ability to interact with clients in a lawyerly way.
Our licensing system cannot credibly claim to protect clients unless it assesses candidates’ ability to interact effectively with them.

kp.k: Issue identification is interactive, critical, and iterative
kp.d: Participants distinguish examination issue spotting from identifying problems through incomplete and changing client accounts. The authors identify three necessary elements: critical thinking, threshold concepts across legal subjects, and effective client interaction. Identifying issues includes both finding possible claims or remedies and detecting obstacles to a resolution; it may require reframing a client’s or supervisor’s initial question.
qs: Clients, on the other hand, tell stories that are complicated and incomplete.
Issue identification in practice is interactive and iterative.

Issue identification in practice requires critical thinking skills, an understanding of threshold concepts in many practice areas, and the ability to interact with a client or supervisor in a way that brings hidden issues to light.

kp.k: Research and interpretation require varied sources and methods
kp.d: The authors identify four research functions: answering legal questions, checking and updating doctrine, acquiring facts and nonlegal knowledge, and discovering local rules or practices. Participants used commercial and free databases, treatises, internal materials, internet searches, and direct inquiries to officials, sometimes selecting methods according to client cost constraints. They also described gaps in statutory, regulatory, and contract interpretation despite greater confidence with judicial opinions. The report treats interpretation, rather than mere access to legal texts, as a source of lawyers’ value.
qs: Lawyers provide value to their clients not because they can access legal materials, but because they know how to interpret them.
To perform this work effectively, focus group members explained that they needed to know both a range of research methods and how to choose the appropriate method for each situation.
our work builds on that consensus by demonstrating that this is not a unidimensional skill; new lawyers must be able to apply research skills in multiple settings and for multiple purposes.

kp.k: Communication requires concision, audience awareness, listening, and negotiation
kp.d: Participants emphasized concise emails and oral explanations, understandable client language, choosing suitable communication channels, attentive reception, and effective negotiation. The report describes email as the dominant written communication form and distinguishes negotiation from adversarial advocacy. New lawyers negotiated with opposing counsel, clients, executives, union representatives, and sometimes outside counsel over budgets; many wished they had received negotiation training.
qs: Emails, for example, have replaced memos and briefs as the dominant form of written communication.
Effective communication requires reception as well as transmission.
Negotiation, they noted, is quite different from advocacy.

kp.k: Professional judgment includes strategy, organization, and collaboration
kp.d: Participants reported that understanding individual rules did not necessarily enable them to manage a matter’s overall trajectory or develop strategy. Gaps in big-picture understanding led to missed steps and transaction delays. Workload competence required time management, organizing documents and matters, and collaboration with supervisors, peers, paralegals, and other staff. Supervisors and juniors emphasized balancing timeliness with quality rather than rewarding speed alone.
qs: These new lawyers knew the rules, but they did not know how to combine the rules into a successful strategy.
They pointed to three components of this building block: careful time management, meticulous organization, and effective collaboration.
The most important aspect of time management for our participants was balancing speed with quality: neither clients nor supervisors appreciated quick work if it was shoddy.

kp.k: Ethical competence requires application, not merely rule knowledge
kp.d: New lawyers reported difficulty recognizing and resolving ethical issues despite studying professional responsibility, including errors concerning privilege, client authority, and disclosures. Some confronted unethical or discriminatory behavior by colleagues, clients, and judges. Supervisors often emphasized commitment, hours, teamwork, and deference, while juniors emphasized unethical or biased conduct. The authors acknowledge those differences without resolving them and separately raise a normative question about whether competence includes responsibility for the quality of justice.
qs: These new lawyers had studied the rules of professional conduct in law school and for the bar exam, but they still struggled to apply those rules in practice.
Supervisors placed a premium on long hours and deference; new lawyers were more concerned about unethical or biased behavior by supervisors, clients, and others.
Our study does not answer that normative question, but it is one for jurisdictions to ponder as they define this first building block of minimum competence.

kp.k: Stress management and self-directed learning protect clients
kp.d: Participants linked practice stress to responsibility for real clients and reported mistakes associated with stress. The authors treat healthy coping as a developable ability, not something demonstrated simply by surviving a stressful examination or appropriately screened through character-and-fitness judgments. Limited training also required new lawyers to organize internal learning, build resource banks, study colleagues’ documents, seek mentors, and recognize when to ask for help.
qs: Coping with stress is an ability that can be developed.
To represent clients competently, they had to take control of their own learning.
Self-directed learning, in other words, requires knowing what you don’t know—as well as possessing the initiative and ingenuity to fill in those gaps.

kp.k: Conventional examination formats poorly reproduce professional work
kp.d: The authors report strong participant criticism of closed-book tests, restrictive time limits, and multiple-choice questions. Critics argued that these emphasize recall and speed, weakly test issue identification, omit communication, and suppress contextual strategy and adversarial argument. A few participants noted real workplace time pressure, but most regarded examination limits as more severe. The authors acknowledge multiple-choice scoring efficiency and reliability while arguing that those benefits cannot compensate for failure to assess needed competence.
qs: Closed-book exams offer a poor measure of minimum competence to practice law.
A few new lawyers challenged this assessment, noting that they sometimes had to respond quickly to client or supervisor demands.
These tests are more efficient to grade than other written formats, which may reduce the expense of licensing exams.
They also aid reliability, which is an important concern in licensing.

kp.k: Performance tests are promising but need redesign
kp.d: Participants generally praised written performance tests using client files and supplied legal materials as resembling first-year work, while criticizing their 90-minute limits. The authors recommend replacing essays with more performance tests, extending time, and potentially including actual research rather than only closed-universe materials. They argue that written examinations can assess at most half the building blocks and must be complemented by other methods.
qs: These performance tests, new lawyers agreed, most closely parallel the work they do during the first year of practice.
Recommendation Three: Eliminate essay questions from written exams and substitute more performance tests.
Performance tests, finally, can be adapted to measure research abilities—a building block that current exams fail to address.

kp.k: AI appears as a limited assessment-cost proposal
kp.d: The report’s explicit AI discussion concerns scoring constructed-response examinations, not changes to legal-service delivery or lawyer employment. Citing assessment research, the authors suggest that AI may reduce scoring costs by limiting the responses requiring human review, while not replacing human graders entirely. This is presented as a promising possibility rather than a result of the focus-group study.
qs: Artificial intelligence has also shown promise in reducing the cost of this scoring—not by replacing human graders entirely but by limiting the number of answers that human graders must review.

kp.k: Clinical education should become a licensing requirement
kp.d: Participants repeatedly credited clinics with preparing them for client work, integrating knowledge, and introducing professional responsibility under supervision. The authors prefer clinics’ combination of realism and pedagogy, while warning that externships and postgraduate apprenticeships may lack adequate supervision. They recommend at least four credits of closely supervised clinical work plus four further clinical or externship credits, ideally increasing over time to at least 15 credits, including eight in closely supervised clinics. These recommendations are not supported by a controlled comparison within this study.
qs: Clinics are the only courses that consistently integrate realism and pedagogy.
Ideally, aspiring lawyers would complete at least 15 credits of clinical work (equivalent to a full semester) before receiving licenses.

We propose here four credits of closely supervised clinical work, complemented by four additional credits of clinical or externship experience, as the bare minimum needed to assure minimum competence.

kp.k: Licensing reform combines coursework, multiple pathways, and evaluation
kp.d: The authors recommend three credits each in client interaction, negotiation, and the lawyer’s public-citizen responsibility for justice. They illustrate test-centered, experience-centered, and diploma-centered systems; the diploma model specifies 69 credits within a JD requiring at least 83 credits, leaving at least 14 elective credits. Jurisdictions could offer multiple pathways. A diverse standing stakeholder group, including clients and students, should review the framework and assess validity, reliability, fairness, and accessibility under universal-design principles.
qs: A jurisdiction could offer candidates two or three pathways to licensure, with each path assessing building blocks in a different manner.
Any implemented licensure process, including those that incorporate recommendations from this study, must also be evaluated to assure validity, reliability, and fairness.
Accessibility for disabled test takers and others should not be an afterthought.

kp.k: Access to justice requires competence without unnecessary exclusion
kp.d: The authors connect licensing to unmet civil legal need, citing research that most civil justice problems never reach lawyers or courts and that approximately three-quarters of state-court civil cases in one study involved at least one self-represented litigant. They caution both against admission barriers that may reduce access and against inadequate preparation that harms vulnerable clients. Participants expressed particular concern about learning essential skills through lightly supervised pro bono representation.
qs: A licensing system that imposes unnecessary barriers to admission may exacerbate the justice gap.
At the same time, a system that fails to screen for key competencies may subject clients, especially the most vulnerable, to poor representation.
New lawyers generally appreciated these opportunities, but they voiced discomfort at learning essential skills by taking responsibility for vulnerable clients.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Merritt and Cornett state that AI shows promise in reducing the cost of scoring constructed-response licensing assessments by reducing the number of answers requiring human review, rather than eliminating human graders.
pts.d: The claim appears in Recommendation Two, which urges jurisdictions to use multiple-choice tests sparingly, if at all. The authors present AI-assisted scoring as a potentially less costly way to assess answers written in candidates’ own words. This is a narrow claim about legal licensing assessment, not a prediction that AI will replace lawyers or transform legal service delivery.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors support the AI-scoring claim with published assessment research, not an AI experiment conducted in their own study.
pts.d: Footnote 480 cites André A. Rupp et al., Automated Essay Scoring at Scale: A Case Study in Switzerland and Germany (2019), and Isaac A. Bejar’s historical survey of research on constructed-response formats, cited previously in footnote 479. The report supplies no numerical cost savings, scoring accuracy results, or demonstration of AI scoring a bar examination. Its focus-group research concerns lawyer competence and licensing; it is not presented as direct evidence of AI performance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: As of October 2020, AI-assisted scoring is described as promising, with no implementation deadline or quantified forecast.
pts.d: The proposed cost benefit concerns constructed-response scoring and explicitly retains human graders. The authors recommend exploring assessment alternatives rather than reporting an established AI-based legal licensing system. More broadly, they require any implemented licensing process to be evaluated for validity, reliability, and fairness.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Licensing authorities and human graders are the immediate affected groups; candidates and the public are indirect stakeholders.
pts.d: Jurisdictions and bar examiners could face lower constructed-response scoring costs, while graders would review fewer answers without being replaced entirely. Candidates could encounter alternative assessment formats if jurisdictions adopted the authors’ broader recommendations. Public protection is the stated purpose of licensing reform, but the report does not claim that AI itself demonstrably improves public protection or lowers candidates’ fees.
